claims.text: SST moved from AWS CDK to Pulumi, unlocking multi-cloud flexibility, faster deployments, and a better developer experience; Pulumi offers a more flexible, provider-agnostic approach to infrastructure management.

Debugging AWS CDK is frustrating because CDK generates CloudFormation templates (an intermediary YAML/JSON format) that are then executed, so the code you write is not the code that runs during deployment.
Multi-cloud deployment was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
The table-of-contents links use the alias path /blog/from-cdk-pulumi-evolution-of-sst/ with anchors matching the post's section headings (e.g., #the-beginnings-of-sst).
SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is essentially a code generator that produces an intermediary format (such as YAML or JSON) which is then executed to deploy the resources.

With AWS CDK, the code a developer writes is not the same as the code running during the deployment process, leading to difficulty debugging, lack of visibility into the deployment process, and challenges extending or customizing the deployment workflow.
The Pulumi docs page at https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/comparisons/cloudformation/ has a section 'what-is-aws-cloudformation'.

The Pulumi docs page at /docs/iac/comparisons/aws-cdk/ has a section (anchor #what-is-aws-cdk) describing the AWS-centric nature of CDK; the CloudFormation comparison page has an anchor #what-is-aws-cloudformation.
Pulumi supports multi-cloud deployment across AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as programming languages (the table marks CDK language support as limited to TypeScript, Python).
Pulumi supports any programming language.

Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment rather than generating an intermediary format; the infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment.
With Pulumi, the infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment, giving greater visibility into the deployment process and the ability to extend or customize it.

Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach allowed SST's team to easily add support for new cloud and on-premises providers, and SST users can manage all their infrastructure through a single, consistent interface without juggling multiple tools.

The SST team's migration from CDK to Pulumi required re-implementing the higher-level components and abstractions built on top of CDK and handling edge cases and complex deployment scenarios from the CDK-based version.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights (https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities into deployments.

Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components that SST leveraged to integrate with cloud and on-premises services and implement complex deployment workflows.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize the deployment process.
With Pulumi, the SST team was able to easily add support for new providers.
With SST built on Pulumi, users can manage all of their infrastructure across multiple cloud providers and on-premises through a single, consistent interface.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy it across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.

The SST team is exploring deeper integration with application frameworks, expanded cloud and on-premises provider support, improved deployment workflows (faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, more granular control), and enhanced observability and monitoring built on Pulumi.
The Pulumi Cloud Deployments docs (/docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/) describe advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Insights provides better visibility into the deployment process and more robust monitoring and observability.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, as described in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand Pulumi workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
The Pulumi Cloud signup page is at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.

A blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi", and it covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from CDK to Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
In SST Ion, constructs (components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, in which constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3 (temporal framing: Ion is described as not yet stable).
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.

SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console; the Console is optional and includes a free tier; SST also potentially earns supplemental income from enterprise services and consulting.
The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.

In SST's deploy chain: SST resolves components from `sst.config.ts` and compiles them into Pulumi resource declarations; the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations; Terraform-bridged providers (via Pulumi's Terraform bridge) translate each resource into cloud API calls; state is written to an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account.
The blog post /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ exists and tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK, from SST's side.
Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
Nitric, a cloud-agnostic application framework, runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine (and its provider bridge) rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed despite the team's broadened attention to opencode, and SST's release cadence has not changed.
The SST team has said repeatedly, about their own architecture, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine.

With SST, you define your app's infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites, etc.), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs page "What is SST" says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
Independent developers who have compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi directly describe the same architecture as SST's own writing (SST built on the Pulumi engine).

Gautier Blandin, in "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis", writes: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."

Kiryl Anoshka, in "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" (dev.to), writes: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more (`@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`), alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.
`sst deploy` reads your `sst.config.ts`, resolves SST's own components, and compiles them into Pulumi resource declarations (a step handled by SST rather than the Pulumi engine).
The Pulumi engine diffs desired versus actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations in an SST deployment.
| Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls | [Pulumi's Terraform bridge](https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) |

Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs underneath SST, while SST owns the CLI, component model, and local dev loop.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding the Pulumi engine for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools, in the same embedding manner SST does.
See the docs page at /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/.
See the blog post at /blog/any-terraform-provider/.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers, adapted for the Pulumi engine, instead of writing their own.

Cross-references exist for the Pulumi docs pages /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/, /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, and the blog posts /blog/any-terraform-provider/ and /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ (the latter described as 'the fuller story of SST's move off CDK, told from SST's side').

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to their users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
- **SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers.** SST's state lives in your own S3 bucket, not in Pulumi's hosted service, and SST doesn't require a Pulumi account to work.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model; SST keeps its own abstractions and API.

Because SST's components compile to Pulumi resources, users can define resources directly in Pulumi inside an SST app for anything lacking a dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app.
The `sst` npm package gets roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026, per the npm downloads API).
opencode (anomalyco/opencode) has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub following (star count) than SST itself, as observed September 2026.
SST is not being abandoned; releases and download numbers indicate continued activity.
Anyone who runs SST is already running Pulumi's engine, whether or not they have written any Pulumi code.

Yes. Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers that are bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.

Yes. SST shipped v4.17.1 in July 2026 and the `sst` package continues to see roughly 796,000 weekly downloads on npm. The team's public attention has broadened to include opencode, an open source AI coding agent, but that hasn't changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.
The docs page /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ exists and explains the engine mechanics.
The blog post /blog/any-terraform-provider/ is titled "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi" and covers the bridge SST and others build on.
The Automation API docs page shows how other tools embed Pulumi the same way SST does.

stances.text: Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK deployments, because CDK is slower due to CloudFormation and Pulumi uses 'faster direct execution'.
AWS CDK is AWS-only for multi-cloud support, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises.
Pulumi is a modern IaC platform that takes a fundamentally different approach to infrastructure management than CDK/CloudFormation.
With CDK/CloudFormation, the intermediary CloudFormation templates often obscured the underlying logic and made problems harder to diagnose.

Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation. In late 2023 the team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced that entire deployment layer. Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported architecture since.
Embedding the Pulumi engine gives a framework like SST a production-grade provisioning engine and hundreds of cloud providers without building either from scratch.
SST isn't the only project to make this choice.
opencode (anomalyco/opencode) has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger following on GitHub (more stars) than SST itself.

SST is a strong fit for an opinionated, full-stack application framework with infrastructure and code defined together, while cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, and infrastructure shared across multiple applications are capabilities SST doesn't expose on its own.
